summary: The filmmaker and author of Terrible Old Games You've Probably Never Heard Of gives us a tour of his Steam library.
body: Disk Cleanup (Image credit: Future) Welcome to Disk Cleanup , our regular weekend feature delving into the PCs of PC gaming luminaries. Come back every weekend to read a new interview, digging into the important questions, like "How tidy is your desktop?" and "What game will you never uninstall?" Stuart Ashen—better known by his YouTube persona Ashens—grew up on a diet of 8-bit games on consoles like the Atari 2600 and the Spectrum. The earliest PC game he recalls playing was Syndicate Wars on his first home-built rig—a Pentium 200 MMX machine housed in a server tower case: "I loved Syndicate . Hated Syndicate Wars. Never got on with it at all," he says. "Ended up giving it to a friend who loved it … I think I went on to Duke Nukem 3D or something." A YouTuber since 2006, Ashens is known primarily for his reviews of weird and (typically not) wonderful food products on his main channel , which to date has 1.67 million subscribers. But he's also a regular critic and commentator on retro video games, both on his twice weekly Ashenscast Twitch stream (which also covers obscure TV and film), and in books like Terrible Old Games You've Probably Never Heard Of . summary: I won't miss.
body: Slay the Spire 2 has a new character—notably, a new character in testing —and as the patch notes themselves point out , that testing will very much be needed: "We expect to make a great number of content and balance changes before the Fool is ready for the main branch." I decided to hop into the beta branch myself and take her for a whirl, and—yeah, those changes'll have to come. The Fool's central mechanic is her bow and arrow—she can fire an arrow/shoot card to deal damage equal to the card's base damage plus her aim. So if a shoot card deals 15 damage and she has six aim stocked, she'll deal 21. This is a little busted, because by default, the Fool has 6 aim already put in her bank. Her non-strike starter card, Foolish Shot, already deals a hefty 15 damage for just one energy. With aim, the first time she uses it, it deals a whopping 21 damage, which is a heck of a damage output for the Fool's first round of combat. The saving grace here is that when a card that fires an arrow is used, that arrow becomes lodged in a target, who gains the Impale status. title: Former survival MMO Dune: Awakening can now be played 'without requiring an Internet connection at any point' as its much requested offline mode arrives
summary: Everything including 'creating and deleting single-player characters' can be done without touching the web.
body: At long last, the transfer of power is complete. Dune: Awakening , Funcom's ambitious survival MMO based on the classic sci-fi novel, has completed is pivot away from massive multiplayer, and can now be played fully offline. The offline function arrived in an otherwise unremarkable patch that mainly fixes specific bugs and technical issues. "It's not possible to play the game in single-player mode without requiring an Internet connection at any point," Funcom revealed in a Steam post. This includes "creating and deleting single-player characters." Dune: Awakening has been gradually drifting away from being a purely multiplayer experience for some time. In April, Funcom made its PvP element, like the Deep Desert and shipwreck exploration, fully optional . A fully fledged single-player mode arrived in September, including a dramatic rework of several major endgame systems—like its dynamic political "Landsraad" system' to make them work in solo play. At that point, single-player still required an Internet connection. Now though, that's no longer the case. To be clear, Dune: Awakening can still be played with all its multiplayer and PvP trappings, now including a "Go Online" button fo…

title: The most annoying questgivers in PC games
summary: The XP isn't worth it.
body: Moira Brown gets a bad rap. Fallout 3's most chipper NPC, the Minnesotan menace is an inventor who sends you out on fact-finding missions to investigate the many dangers of the Wasteland. That means she puts you in harm's way quite a lot, which many players hate her for. Others just hate her voice. I think her positive outlook makes a refreshing change of pace from, you know, everything else going on in Fallout 3. Plus she gives you an armored Vault suit just for starting her questline, and the Wasteland Survival Guide she writes with your help goes on to be a useful item in both New Vegas and Fallout 4. What I'm saying is, there are plenty of videogame questgivers much more annoying than Moira Brown. All of the ones below, for starters. And if you disagree, you're a big meanie. Zero isn't alone—in GTA: San Andreas, he's got wannabe MC/janitor OG Loc for competition—but he is the winner for absolute worst. title: Is the game funny, or just the players? Jackbox CEO says they get 'a lot of false positives' with a staff of comedy writers
summary: Testing comedy games comes with a unique challenge.
body: Social improv games like those in Jackbox 's Party Packs can have vastly different vibes depending on who you're playing with. Meemaw isn't likely to appreciate the phrase "glup shitto" the way your PC gaming friends will, and those sorts of high-variance dynamics are something Jackbox Games has to stay acutely aware of, according to CEO Mike Bilder. "I mean we do a ton [of testing] internally, but then as games get greenlit, we'll bring in external groups," Bilder told PC Gamer associate editor Ted Litchfield in a recent interview. "We want to make sure that we're not just local-biased with our own opinions on things. We want to make sure these games are playing well." Something that makes it especially hard to tell whether a game is funny or they're just having a good session is the fact that they work with comedy writers—people who can make a boring game seem funny just by cracking jokes while they play. "We get a lot of false positives because we have such funny people here that work in the office, and they make games shine," said Bilder. title: Do you like mob tagging in oldschool MMOs, or are you done with fighting for quest credit?
summary: Tag, you're it.
body: Terminally Online (Image credit: Future) This is Terminally Online : PC Gamer's very own MMO column. Every other week, I'll be sharing my thoughts on the genre, interviewing fellow MMO-heads like me, taking a deep-dive into mechanics we've all taken for granted, and, occasionally, bringing in guest writers to talk about their MMO of choice. I've been having a pleasant time with WoW: Forever (and by that, I mean it has consumed nearly every waking moment of my life). One thing, however, has been made pretty clear: Mob tagging, that is, only giving kill credit to the first player (or group) to damage a mob, is divisive. One side of the fence—my side, I'm afraid—does see mob tagging as a necessary evil in an MMO that's trying to drive social interaction. Videogames, particularly ones that are incentivising you to group up, are kind of meant to be a pain in the butt sometimes; if you've got a "kill 20" quest and there another person there, the fact you might get in each other's way if you don't group up, and have a jollier time if you do, is a net good. summary: "On one hand, I want to pay off those expectations. On the other hand, I want to exceed them."
body: Harvey Smith remembers the 10 months he spent as quality assurance lead on System Shock as a "brush with greatness". "I had loved Ultima Underworld, and then I got to work with the very people that were rolling off of Underworld onto this new cyberpunk game," he says. "Looking Glass fought like cats and dogs, but man, they were passionate about what they were doing. And this was a mission for them." (Image credit: Nightdive) Afterwards, when Smith joined System Shock producer Warren Spector at Ion Storm Austin, "we just applied that same hunger to Deus Ex ," he says. "And then when I got together with Raphaël Colantonio, we were like, 'Why just live a normal life? Why fucking punch in and sit at a desk and run some numbers? We're just dying to do this, right?' And so we made Dishonored ." It's a simplified take on the story—one that skips the wilderness years spent fighting for funding before Arkane partnered with Bethesda. But the stubborn and single-minded outlook Smith describes is crucial to explaining his career in immersive sims. title: A survival game we once called 'Stalker and Tarkov's alien baby' is closing down less than a year after launch
summary: Pioner seemed headed in the right direction when it went into early access in late 2025, but it all went wrong just a few months later.
body: Pioner, a survival-shooter we said looked like " Stalker and Tarkov's alien baby " when we first laid eyes on it in 2021, is ending development and closing down. In an announcement posted today on Steam, developer GFAGames said further work on the game and continued operation of its servers requires more money, and it just doesn't have any. "Over the past few months, we have been in talks with existing and potential partners about investment and new ways of working together that would allow us to preserve the project and the team," the studio wrote. "We were unable to agree on the funding needed to continue the project. The studio no longer has sufficient funds of its own to continue development and keep the servers running." Pioner looked promising when it turned up at the PC Gaming Show in 2021: A mash-up of Stalker, Metro, and Escape From Tarkov that featured both a singleplayer campaign and online co-op and PvP survival action, all of it built around late Soviet-era technology. title: AMD has patched its SSD-eating GPU driver bug with an optional Adrenalin update for RX 7000-series graphics cards and above
summary: It looks like it's got some quirks of its own, though.
body: I reported earlier this week on a bug within AMD's GPU driver suite , wherein a misfiring utility was accused of making huge amounts of erroneous storage writes. Some AMD graphics card owners reported their SSD health dropping by up to 1% per month, but a fix has finally arrived. AMD Adrenalin Edition 26.11.1 is an optional update, which means you'll need to download the installer yourself. However, according to the topline notes, the update fixes "excessive writes to the system drive" at idle for Radeon RX 7000-series graphics cards and above. AMD's wording suggests that older GPUs might not be affected by the bug, but some of the user reports mention RX 6000-series cards, so it's unclear if a fix for earlier models is still in the works. I also think it's a slightly odd move to make this an "optional" update, given the severity of some of the reports, though this is often how AMD deals with getting fixes out in between official driver releases—by the looks of the known issues, this interim driver might still need some work before it's patched into the next full release. title: Paradox Interactive is getting a new boss as Fredrik Wester steps down for the second time
summary: Deputy CEO Mattias Lilja is taking the reins in January.
body: Paradox Interactive is getting a new boss: Deputy CEO Mattias Lilja will take over from current CEO Fredrik Wester in January 2027, a move Paradox said "is a natural evolution of how the company is already led." "My plan was never to be CEO for life. The goal was to build the foundation before passing the baton on for the next chapter in the company’s journey," Wester said in today's announcement . "Since I returned as CEO, we’ve streamlined our strategy, rebuilt our pipeline and developed our commercial offering. Mattias has had a central role in laying this foundation, and now is the right time to hand over. Given his experience and vision, he is exceptionally well positioned to take the company to its next level." As his statement implies, this is his second tenure as Paradox CEO: He held the position from 2009 to 2018, when he resigned and was replaced by Ebba Ljungerud. But Ljungerud's tenure was rocky, and she resigned in 2021 over "differing views on the company's strategy going forward," at which point Wester returned to the role. title: Now Jensen's gone, Intel’s trouble finding a steady CEO should serve as cautionary tale to Nvidia’s board
summary: Huang's permanent replacement will have some massive shoes to fill.
body: Has there ever been a tech CEO quite like Jensen Huang? The Nvidia chief has been an emblematic figure to PC gamers for years, before transcending into one of the primary architects of the AI revolution. Regardless of whether you love or hate the technology, (and the financial behemoth that Nvidia has become), you have to admit that Huang has presided over a meteoric rise to the top, the likes of which the tech world has rarely seen. Now Huang, the Nvidia cofounder, figurehead, and global AI industry pillar, has announced his resignation . The admission of an affair with someone some people suspect to be a Chinese spy, followed days later by reports of another affair with an Nvidia employee, proved to be his undoing as Nvidia chief. Nvidia's share price has dropped significantly in recent weeks. Investors, likely looking for some sort of stability after the past few weeks of AI and tech company financial woes, seem shaken. In many ways, the situation is unprecedented, and it's hard to draw parallels. But now Huang has gone, it puts Nvidia in the unenviable position of finding someone to replace him at the top of the stack. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO for…

title: Nvidia stocks jump back up after ex-CEO Jensen Huang's ousting
summary: Nvidia's share price has seemingly grown by around 10% since pre-market trading lows.
body: This week has been a mess for Nvidia, with its CEO, Jensen Huang, admitting to an affair on Sunday , only for a second affair allegation to come out yesterday . Today, Nvidia shares started as low as $151 in pre-market trading, but have since bounced back to between $163 and $166 in the opening hours of Nasdaq trading after the announcement of Jensen Huang's retirement as CEO . One might assume a downward trajectory with Huang's resignation, and CFO Colette Kress replacing him, as it could flag instability to shareholders, but the stock price now sits where it once sat on Wednesday, November 11 at 5 PM ET. The Nvidia stock price has been unruly this week, dipping by $15 between Friday night and Monday morning, then climbing to $181 by the end of Monday, then once again dropping to $167 on Tuesday. But, importantly, this morning saw the worst trade open for Nvidia stock since June 2025, just before the memory crisis started. The jump from $151 to around $165 represents a 10% increase for the company.
